opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot. The core tension is that research benefits from a lot of bottom-up exploration. Some of the best ideas come from people just following their curiosity. But at the scale we're at, if you don't make clear bets, you spread compute and talent too thin and nothing gets the critical mass it needs to really work.

So the way I approach it is to be pretty opinionated at the top level about a small number of big directions. Those are the places where we think the frontier is going to move, and where we're willing to put serious resources behind it. I try to be very explicit about what those priorities are and, just as importantly, what they're not. Saying no to things is a big part of the job, and it's often the hardest part, because there are always more promising ideas than we can fund properly.

Within those directions, though, I really try to push ownership down to the managers and the leads. They're much closer to the work. They know which experiments are actually working, which people are on fire about an idea, where the bottlenecks are. I don't think it scales, and frankly I don't think it's healthy, for me to be making those calls. My role is more to set context: here's why this bet matters, here's roughly how much compute and headcount it gets, here's what success looks like on some time horizon. Then I trust them to figure out the how.

The other piece is keeping a bit of slack in the system for exploration. Not everything should be top-down. We want people to have room to try weird things, because a lot of the paradigm shifts we've seen started as someone's side project that didn't look like a priority at the time. So part of empowering managers is making sure they feel they have permission to protect some of that exploratory work on their teams, and then having a clear path for those ideas to get scaled up when they show signal.

And then there's a lot of communication. I spend a lot of time with the leads just syncing on what we're seeing, where we might need to reallocate, what's surprising us. Research is non-stationary. A bet that looked right six months ago might need to change. So the focus isn't static. It's a continuous conversation, and the managers are really partners in shaping it, not just executing on it.

r001.rationale: The response describes concentrating serious resources on a small number of major research directions and explicitly says those priorities receive compute allocations, communicating the core idea of focusing compute on selected bets.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that research is fundamentally a bet on people. You can't centrally plan your way to the next big breakthrough. If you look at the history of the field, the things that actually moved the needle, whether that's scaling, or RL on reasoning, or whatever comes next, they almost always started as something a small group was convinced of before it was obvious to everyone else. So my job isn't really to pick the ideas. It's to pick the people, give them enough room, and then make sure the organization is set up so that when something starts working, we can pour resources on it fast.

That said, you do have to focus. We're not infinitely resourced, compute is the scarcest thing we have, and if you let a thousand flowers bloom with no prioritization you just end up with a thousand half-finished projects. So the way I think about it is at the top level we have a small number of directions we're really betting the company on, and within those directions I try to be very explicit about what the goal is and what "winning" looks like, and then stay out of the way on how.

Empowering managers to me means a couple of concrete things. One is giving them real ownership over their compute allocation and their roadmap, not having every decision route through me. If a lead comes to me and says "I want to spend my budget on this, and I know it looks weird," my default is yes, because they're closer to the problem than I am. Two is being clear about the bar. The thing I try to communicate is that we care about results, we care about rigor, and we care about things that compound. If you hold people to that standard you don't actually need to micromanage the day to day.

The other piece that I think people underrate is taste. A lot of what I do is spend time talking to researchers, looking at results, and trying to build an intuition for which bets are real and which ones are just interesting. And then I try to push that taste down into the org, so the managers themselves are developing good judgment about what to fund and what to kill. Killing things is honestly the harder half. Everyone wants to start projects. Deciding something isn't going to work and reallocating those people and that compute, that's where a lot of the leverage is, and it's where I lean on managers the most, because if I'm the only one who can make those calls we don't scale.

And then the last thing I'd say is that we try to keep a pretty tight loop between research and what actually ships. Not because every project needs to turn into a product, but because deployment gives you signal. It tells you where the models are actually falling down for real people, and that feeds back into what we should be betting on next. So the focus isn't a static thing, it's something we're updating constantly based on what the models and the users are telling us.

r001.rationale: The response says OpenAI makes a small number of major research bets and that compute is scarce, but it does not clearly advocate allocating large blocks of compute to those selected bets.

astra-6.text:
I think about it as balancing focus with room to explore. You want a small number of priorities that people understand—what we’re trying to achieve and why those problems matter. But if you prescribe every step, you lose a lot of the value of having strong researchers and managers.

So I want managers to have ownership over how their teams pursue those priorities, including the ability to challenge the assumptions behind them. The conversation should be about what they’re learning, what evidence would change our minds, and where they need help—not just whether they’re executing a fixed plan.

Research is uncertain. You need enough conviction to give an idea time to work, but enough flexibility to change direction when the evidence calls for it. Clear priorities and real autonomy can reinforce each other.

r001.rationale: The response discusses clear priorities and manager autonomy, but does not advocate allocating large blocks of compute to selected major research bets.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it as setting a clear direction without trying to make every decision myself. We need a shared view of the biggest problems and where a breakthrough would matter most. But the people closest to the research need room to decide how to attack those problems—and to tell me when our assumptions are wrong.

With managers, I want to agree on what we’re trying to learn, what resources they need, and what evidence would make us change course. Then they should have real ownership. If every consequential decision comes back to me, I haven’t actually empowered them.

There’s a balance between concentrating enough effort to make progress and leaving room for something surprising. You want people to have the freedom to pursue an unexpected result, while being willing to stop work that’s no longer promising. The conversations should be about the evidence and the opportunity, rather than defending a plan just because we committed to it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses prioritizing important problems and concentrating effort, but it does not say to allocate large blocks of compute to selected research bets.
